source: English Grammar for Students of Italian (Adorni & Primorac, 2nd ed.), modernised: voi for groups, gli for 'to them', visto, Cos'è.

questions.q: Tu or Lei: which 'you' do I use?
questions.a: Use tu with friends, family, children and anyone you call by first name. Use Lei with strangers, shopkeepers, officials and anyone you'd call signore or signora; when in doubt, use Lei.

examples.en: Good morning, madam, how are you?

questions.q: Why does the polite 'you' look like 'she'?
questions.a: Lei, the polite 'you', takes the same verb form as lei (she). Context tells you which one is meant.

questions.q: Why do Italians say 'sto bene' and not 'sono bene'?
questions.a: How you are in health is expressed with stare, not essere. So 'I'm fine' is sto bene and 'How are you?' is come stai? or come sta?

examples.en: How are you? I'm fine, thanks.

questions.q: Why 'la signora Rossi' with 'the'?
questions.a: When you talk about someone, a title like signora, signor or dottore takes the article. When you speak to them directly, drop it.

examples.it: La signora Rossi è molto gentile.

questions.q: How do I make a sentence negative?
questions.a: Put non right before the verb. There's nothing else to add.

questions.q: Where is 'do' or 'did' in an Italian negative?
questions.a: Nowhere: Italian has no word for 'do/does/did'. Non plus the verb does the whole job.

questions.q: How do I say 'slowly' or 'clearly'?
questions.a: Many adverbs are made by adding -mente to the feminine adjective (lenta → lentamente, chiara → chiaramente). Adverbs never change their ending.

questions.q: Why does 'come si dice?' use si?
questions.a: Si plus a verb means 'one' or 'people' in general, so come si dice? is literally 'how does one say?'.

examples.en: How do you say 'fork' in Italian?

questions.q: Do I need to say 'io', 'tu', 'lui'?
questions.a: Usually not: the verb ending already says who. Add the pronoun only for emphasis or contrast, or to make clear who in the third person.

questions.q: How do I ask a yes/no question?
questions.a: Say the sentence with your voice rising at the end. You can also put the subject after the verb; there's no 'do' to add.

questions.q: Why is it 'mi chiamo Josh'?
questions.a: Chiamarsi means 'to call oneself', so Italians say 'I call myself Josh'. The mi is part of the verb and can't be dropped.

examples.it: Mi chiamo Josh. E tu, come ti chiami?
examples.en: My name's Josh. And what's your name?

questions.q: Why 'americana' for a woman and 'americano' for a man?
questions.a: Italian adjectives match the gender and number of the person or thing. Adjectives in -o have four forms (-o, -a, -i, -e); adjectives in -e have two (-e, -i).

questions.q: Why 'l'Italia' with an article?
questions.a: Countries usually take the article (l'Italia, gli Stati Uniti), but after in for 'in/to a country' the article normally drops.

examples.it: Abito in Italia da un mese.
examples.en: I've been living in Italy for a month.

questions.q: 'To Rome' or 'in Rome': a or in?
questions.a: Cities take a, countries and regions take in. The same word covers 'to' and 'in'.

questions.q: Che, che cosa or cosa?
questions.a: All three mean 'what?' and are interchangeable; cosa is the most common in speech.

questions.q: Why is a table feminine?
questions.a: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, and for things the choice is arbitrary. Learn each noun with its article so you learn its gender too.

questions.q: How can I tell if a noun is masculine or feminine?
questions.a: The ending usually tells you: -o is masculine, -a feminine, a consonant masculine, and -zione, -tà feminine. Nouns in -e can be either, so learn them with il or la.

questions.q: Why 'il problema' if -a is feminine?
questions.a: A few nouns break the pattern: il problema and il programma are masculine, la mano is feminine. These have to be learned one by one.

questions.q: Why 'uno spritz' but 'un caffè'?
questions.a: Masculine words starting with z or s + consonant take uno; other masculine words take un. Feminine words take una, or un' before a vowel.

examples.it: Uno spritz e un caffè, per favore.
examples.en: A spritz and a coffee, please.
An orange soda and a fresh juice.

questions.q: How do I make a noun plural?
questions.a: Change the last vowel: -o and -e become -i, -a becomes -e. Nouns ending in an accented vowel or a consonant don't change.

questions.q: Why 'due caffè' and not 'due caffèi'?
questions.a: Nouns ending in an accented vowel or a consonant are the same in the plural; the article or number shows it's plural.

questions.q: How do I say 'it' as a subject?
questions.a: You don't say it: the verb alone is enough. Italian has no everyday word for 'it' as a subject.

questions.q: How do I ask politely for something?
questions.a: Use vorrei (I would like) or a conditional like potrebbe (could you). Mi dà...? and posso avere...? also work at the counter.

questions.q: How do I say 'a coffee cup' or 'orange juice'?
questions.a: Italian doesn't stack nouns. It says noun + da/di/a + noun: 'a cup for coffee', 'juice of orange'. Da shows what something is for, di what it's made of.

questions.q: How do I say 'I'm 30'?
questions.a: Age uses avere: 'I have thirty years'. Ask with quanti anni hai?

questions.q: Why are there so many words for 'the'?
questions.a: 'The' has to match the noun's gender, its number and its first sound: il, lo, l', la in the singular; i, gli, le in the plural.

examples.it: il pane, lo zucchero, l'olio, la pasta
examples.en: the bread, the sugar, the oil, the pasta

examples.it: i biscotti, gli spaghetti, le uova
examples.en: the biscuits, the spaghetti, the eggs

questions.q: When do I use lo and gli?
questions.a: Lo (plural gli) goes before masculine words starting with z, s + consonant, gn, ps or y. Before a vowel, the masculine singular is l' and the plural is gli.

questions.q: How do I say 'some'?
questions.a: Use di + 'the': del, dello, della, dell', dei, degli, delle. Un po' di also works for 'a bit of'.

questions.q: Why is there no 'del' in 'non ho pane'?
questions.a: The 'some' word is dropped after non, and it's optional in questions.

examples.it: Avete pane? No, oggi non abbiamo pane.
examples.en: Do you have any bread? No, we don't have any bread today.
I don't have any friends here.

questions.q: C'è or ecco?
questions.a: C'è / ci sono says something exists or is somewhere. Ecco points at it: 'here it is!' or 'there it is!' and needs no verb.

examples.en: Is there a pharmacy near here?

questions.q: How do I say 'this one' or 'that one'?
questions.a: Just questo or quello, matched to the noun you mean. There's no word for 'one'.

examples.en: Which cake would you like? This one.

questions.q: How do I ask 'what is it?' when I don't know a word?
questions.a: Use Cos'è? for 'what is it?' and Cosa sono? for several things. Cos'è is for a definition; for a choice, use qual è.

questions.q: How do I say 'look for'?
questions.a: Cercare already means 'look for', so don't add a preposition. Many English verb + preposition pairs are one Italian verb.

questions.q: C'è or è?
questions.a: C'è asks or says whether something exists (is there a...?). È with dov'è asks where a specific thing is.

questions.q: How do I say 'to Luca's' or 'to the doctor's'?
questions.a: Use da + the person: it means 'to' or 'at someone's place'.

examples.en: Tonight we're having dinner at Luca's.

questions.q: Why 'entrare in' when English just says 'enter'?
questions.a: Some Italian verbs need a preposition where English has none (entrare in, avvicinarsi a). Learn each verb with its preposition.

questions.q: Why do directions sound like 'giri' and 'prenda' instead of 'gira' and 'prendi'?
questions.a: Those are polite (Lei) commands, and they borrow the subjunctive's vowels: -are verbs end in -i, -ere and -ire verbs in -a. Scusi, senta and mi dica work the same way.

examples.it: Giri a destra e prenda la seconda.
examples.en: Turn right and take the second one.
Yes, how can I help you?

questions.q: Che or quale before a noun?
questions.a: Che + noun is a general 'what'; quale + noun means 'which one of these'. In everyday speech che is used for both.

questions.q: Why 'quante mele' but 'quanto pane'?
questions.a: Quanto (how much / how many) matches the noun: quanto, quanta, quanti, quante. It does this even when the noun is left out.

examples.en: How many peaches would you like?

examples.it: Ho del pane. Quanto ne vuoi?
examples.en: I've got some bread. How much do you want?

questions.q: Why 'l'uovo' but 'le uova'?
questions.a: A few nouns become feminine in the plural, ending in -a: l'uovo → le uova, il braccio → le braccia.

questions.q: 'What's your number?': che or qual è?
questions.a: When the answer is a choice among many (number, address, favourite), use qual è. Use cos'è only to ask for a definition. For a name, say come ti chiami?

questions.q: How do I say 'I like'?
questions.a: Use mi piace: what you like is the subject, so the sentence is really 'it is pleasing to me'. Mi piace for one thing or a verb, mi piacciono for several.

questions.q: Why 'mi piacciono' and not 'mi piace' with plurals?
questions.a: The verb agrees with the thing liked, not with you. Several things are pleasing, so piacciono.

questions.q: How do I say 'it's cold' or 'it's hot'?
questions.a: Weather uses fare: fa freddo, fa caldo, fa bel tempo. È freddo describes a thing, like a coffee.

questions.q: How do I add 'isn't it?' or 'don't you?'
questions.a: Add vero? or no? to the end. Unlike English, it never changes.

questions.q: How do I say 'you all'?
questions.a: Use voi, with the verb in -ate, -ete, -ite. Today voi is used for any group, even polite; the old formal Loro is ceremonial and rare.

examples.en: Gentlemen, are you coming with me?

questions.q: Which verb form goes with 'Maria and I' or 'you and Paolo'?
questions.a: 'X and I' takes the noi form; 'you and X' takes the voi form; two other people take the loro form.

examples.it: Io e Maria andiamo al mare.
examples.en: Maria and I are going to the seaside.
Are you and Paolo coming tonight?

questions.q: Why 'mi piace il caffè' with 'the'?
questions.a: Italian uses the article with nouns meant in general (coffee in general, life, war) where English leaves it out.

questions.q: How do I translate 'reading' in 'I like reading' or 'Reading is fun'?
questions.a: Use the infinitive: leggere. After piacere, after a preposition, and as a subject, English -ing is an Italian infinitive.

questions.q: Buono or bene?
questions.a: Buono is an adjective and describes things (good). Bene is an adverb and describes how something is done (well); it never changes.

questions.q: Does 'molto' change?
questions.a: Only when it means 'many/much' before a noun (molti, molta, molte). As 'very' or 'a lot' it stays molto.

examples.en: There are a lot of people.

examples.it: È molto bello. Mi piace molto.
examples.en: It's very nice. I like it a lot.

questions.q: Is 'can' always potere?
questions.a: For a skill you've learned, use sapere: so nuotare. Use potere for being able or allowed to do something.

examples.it: So nuotare, ma oggi non posso.
examples.en: I can swim, but I can't today.

questions.q: Why 'voglio partire' with no 'to'?
questions.a: The infinitive already means 'to leave'. After volere, potere, dovere and sapere it follows directly.

questions.q: Can I use the present for the future?
questions.a: Yes. For plans and anything soon, the present is normal: domani parto.

questions.q: Can I end a question with a preposition?
questions.a: No. The preposition always goes first: 'with whom are you going?'.

questions.q: How do I say 'with me' or 'for you'?
questions.a: After a preposition use me, te, lui, lei, Lei, noi, voi, loro. Only me and te differ from the subject words.

questions.q: How do I say 'wait for', 'look at' or 'pay for'?
questions.a: Aspettare, guardare and pagare already include the preposition, so they take the thing directly.

questions.q: How do I say 'tickets are sold here' or 'English spoken'?
questions.a: Italians prefer si + verb to the passive. The verb agrees with what follows: si vende for one thing, si vendono for several.

questions.q: Why is the subject after the verb in 'arriva l'autobus'?
questions.a: Italian word order is freer than English. With verbs like arrivare, the subject often comes last. Find the subject by asking who or what is acting.

questions.q: How do I say 'I'm hungry' or 'I'm cold'?
questions.a: These use avere: 'I have hunger', 'I have cold'. The same goes for sete (thirsty), sonno (sleepy), paura (afraid) and caldo (hot).

questions.q: How do I say 'my head hurts'?
questions.a: Say mi fa male + the body part, which is literally 'it does me harm'. Use mi fanno male for plurals, or ho mal di + the body part.

questions.q: Avere or essere in the past?
questions.a: Verbs that take a direct object use avere. Reflexive verbs and most verbs of motion or change (andare, venire, arrivare, partire, uscire, nascere, morire, diventare, restare, stare, essere) use essere.

questions.q: Why 'andata' and not 'andato'?
questions.a: With essere, the past participle matches the subject's gender and number: andato, andata, andati, andate.

questions.q: Is 'I went' or 'I have gone' a different Italian tense?
questions.a: No. 'I went', 'I have gone' and 'I did go' are all the passato prossimo when they mean a finished event.

examples.en: I saw / I've seen the Colosseum.

questions.q: How do I say 'John's'?
questions.a: Italian has no 's. Say 'the X of John': la macchina di Giovanni. With a noun, di joins the article: del, della, dei.

questions.q: How do I ask 'whose'?
questions.a: Say 'of whom is it?': di chi è? for one thing, di chi sono? for several.

questions.q: How do I say 'Mario's' or 'my father's' without a noun?
questions.a: Use quello / quella / quelli / quelle di: 'the one of Mario'. Quello matches the thing you mean.

examples.it: Quale casa vendi? Quella di mio padre.
examples.en: Which house are you selling? My father's.

examples.it: Le mie scarpe? No, quelle di Anna.

questions.q: Why does 'his' become 'sua'?
questions.a: An Italian possessive matches the thing owned, not the owner. So a man's car is la sua macchina, and i suoi libri can mean his books or her books.

questions.q: Do I need 'the' with mio?
questions.a: Yes, normally: il mio libro, la mia casa. But drop it with one family member (mia madre, tuo fratello). It comes back in the plural (i miei fratelli) and always with loro.

questions.q: How do I say 'mine' or 'yours'?
questions.a: Use the same word as 'my' or 'your' with the article and no noun: il mio, la tua, i nostri. It matches the thing, not the owner.

examples.it: Non prendo la tua macchina, prendo la mia.
examples.en: I won't take your car, I'll take mine.

examples.it: I nostri figli stanno bene. E i vostri?
examples.en: Our kids are fine. And yours?

questions.q: Why 'è mio' with no article?
questions.a: After essere, a possessive that just says who owns something usually drops the article.

questions.q: Do adjectives go before or after the noun?
questions.a: Usually after, especially colours, nationalities and shapes. A few common ones (bello, buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo) often go before.

questions.q: Is 'la famiglia' singular or plural?
questions.a: Singular, as in English: a group noun takes a singular verb.

questions.q: How do I say 'I'm doing X'?
questions.a: Usually with the plain present: faccio means 'I do' and 'I'm doing'. Use sto + -ando/-endo only for something happening right this minute.

examples.en: What are you doing? I'm cooking.

questions.q: Why 'mi alzo' for 'I get up'?
questions.a: Many everyday verbs are reflexive in Italian (alzarsi, vestirsi, sedersi, trovarsi), and the mi, ti or si is required. It goes before the verb.

examples.en: How are you getting on in Bologna?

questions.q: Why 'mi sono alzato' with essere?
questions.a: All reflexive verbs take essere in the past, and the participle matches the subject.

examples.en: This morning I got up late.

questions.q: How do I say 'to have a good time'?
questions.a: Use divertirsi. Idioms don't translate word for word: 'avere un buon tempo' means nothing in Italian.

questions.q: Why is 'non vedo nessuno' correct?
questions.a: Italian requires a double negative: non + verb + nessuno, niente or mai. A positive word like qualcosa can't follow non.

questions.q: How do I say 'ever' and 'never'?
questions.a: Both are mai. In a question it means 'ever'; with non it means 'never'.

examples.en: Have you ever been to Venice?

examples.it: Non sono mai stato a Venezia.

questions.q: How do I say 'he likes' or 'she likes'?
questions.a: Use gli piace (to him) and le piace (to her), or a + name: a Marco piace. The verb still agrees with the thing liked.

questions.q: How do I say 'I liked it'?
questions.a: Piacere takes essere in the past, and the participle matches the thing liked: mi è piaciuto, mi è piaciuta, mi sono piaciuti.

examples.it: Mi è piaciuta molto la cena.

questions.q: Passato prossimo or imperfetto?
questions.a: The passato prossimo tells what happened. The imperfetto tells what used to happen, what was going on, and what things were like (age, weather, time, feelings); English 'went' gives no clue.

examples.en: Yesterday I went to the seaside.

examples.it: Da bambino andavo al mare ogni estate.
examples.en: As a child I used to go to the seaside every summer.

questions.q: How do I say 'used to' or 'was doing'?
questions.a: Both are the imperfetto: one word, no extra helper.

examples.en: I used to play football every afternoon.
He was reading when I arrived.

questions.q: How do I say 'before leaving'?
questions.a: Use prima di + infinitive. After any preposition, English -ing is an Italian infinitive.

examples.it: Prima di uscire, chiudo le finestre.
examples.en: Before going out, I close the windows.

questions.q: How do I say 'I remember'?
questions.a: Ricordarsi di: the thing remembered comes after di. Ricordare with a direct object also works.

examples.it: Non mi ricordo del suo nome.

questions.q: Where do object pronouns go?
questions.a: Before the conjugated verb: lo vedo, la prendo. After an infinitive they can attach to its end: posso assaggiarlo.

questions.q: Lo or la for 'it'?
questions.a: 'It' takes the gender of the noun it stands for: lo for masculine, la for feminine. 'Them' is li or le.

examples.it: Vedi la macchina? Sì, la vedo.
examples.en: Do you see the car? Yes, I see it.
The peaches? I'll take them all.

questions.q: Why 'l'ho vista' and not 'l'ho visto'?
questions.a: With avere, the participle matches a lo, la, li or le placed before it. With no pronoun in front, it stays -o.

examples.it: Hai visto Maria? Sì, l'ho vista.
examples.en: Have you seen Maria? Yes, I saw her.

examples.it: Le chiavi? Le ho prese io.

questions.q: Gli or le?
questions.a: Gli means 'to him' (and in speech 'to them'); le means 'to her'; Le means 'to you' formally.

questions.q: How do I say 'to them'?
questions.a: In everyday Italian, gli before the verb. Loro after the verb is correct but formal.

examples.en: I'll give them the keys tomorrow.

examples.it: Ho telefonato ai miei: gli ho detto tutto.
examples.en: I called my parents: I told them everything.

questions.q: Why 'telefono a Maria'?
questions.a: Telefonare takes a, so its pronoun is the 'to' kind: gli or le, not lo or la. Always check what the Italian verb takes, not the English one.

examples.it: Telefono a mia madre ogni giorno.
examples.en: I call my mother every day.

questions.q: Why 'mi dispiace' and not 'io dispiaccio'?
questions.a: Dispiacere works like piacere: the thing is 'displeasing to me'. Mancare, servire and occorrere work the same way.

examples.it: Le dispiace se apro la finestra?
examples.en: Do you mind if I open the window?

questions.q: How do I say 'Who are you talking to?'
questions.a: Put the a first: 'to whom are you speaking?'. The same goes for da chi, con chi and per chi.

examples.it: Da chi hai avuto questo libro?
examples.en: Who did you get this book from?

questions.q: Where does the person go in 'I give Maria the book'?
questions.a: Italian has no 'give someone something' order. Say the thing first, then a + the person: 'I give the book to Maria'.

examples.it: Scrivo una lettera a mio fratello.
examples.en: I'm writing my brother a letter.

questions.q: How do I stress 'HER, not him'?
questions.a: Use the strong pronoun after the verb (vedo lei, ho dato il libro a lei) instead of the short one before it.

examples.en: I'm not looking for him, I'm looking for her.

examples.it: L'ho dato a te, non a lui.
examples.en: I gave it to you, not to him.

questions.q: How do I find the Italian for 'look after' or 'look into'?
questions.a: Look up the whole English phrase: each has its own Italian verb (badare a, approfondire). Never take the first meaning of 'look' and add a preposition.

questions.q: How do I tell a friend 'don't'?
questions.a: For tu, use non + the infinitive: non toccare, non preoccuparti. For everyone else, just put non before the command.

questions.q: How do I say 'let's'?
questions.a: Use the noi form of the verb, with no extra word.

questions.q: How do I form the future?
questions.a: Drop the final -e of the infinitive and add -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno; -are verbs change -ar- to -er-. Some stems are short: andrò, avrò, sarò.

questions.q: Why the future after 'when' or 'as soon as'?
questions.a: If the action is in the future, Italian uses the future in both halves, where English uses the present after 'when'. In casual speech both halves can also be in the present.

examples.en: When you arrive, I'll call you.
As soon as he gets back, I'll call him.

questions.q: Why 'sarà a casa' for 'he's probably home'?
questions.a: Italian uses the future to guess about the present, so you don't need 'probably' or 'I wonder'.

examples.it: Che ore saranno? Saranno le tre.
examples.en: I wonder what time it is. It must be about three.
Who could be at the door?

questions.q: How do I say 'if I have time, I'll come'?
questions.a: For a real possibility, use the present in both parts or the future in both parts.

examples.en: If I have time, I'll come.
If I have time, I'll come.

questions.q: Is there a word for 'will'?
questions.a: No. The future ending carries 'will', and the present often does the job too.

questions.q: How do I say 'taller than', 'the tallest' and 'very tall'?
questions.a: Più alto di (taller than), il più alto (the tallest), altissimo or molto alto (very tall). There's no -er or -est.

examples.it: Roma è più grande di Firenze.

questions.q: 'The best in town': in or di?
questions.a: After a superlative, 'in' or 'of' is always di: il migliore della città, il più bravo della classe.

examples.it: È il ristorante migliore della città.
examples.en: It's the best restaurant in town.

examples.it: È la più piccola della famiglia.
examples.en: She's the youngest in the family.

questions.q: How do I say 'better' and 'worse'?
questions.a: Migliore and peggiore as adjectives (or più buono, più cattivo). As adverbs, use meglio and peggio.

questions.q: How do I form the conditional?
questions.a: Take the future stem and add -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero: parlerei, vorrei, potrebbe.

questions.q: Does 'would' always mean the conditional?
questions.a: No. 'Would' meaning 'used to' is the imperfetto, and 'said he would come' is the past conditional. Otherwise it's the conditional.

examples.it: Quando ero piccolo, mio nonno mi raccontava delle storie.
examples.en: When I was little, my grandfather would tell me stories.

questions.q: How do I say 'you should'?
questions.a: Use the conditional of dovere: dovresti, dovrebbe.

questions.q: How do I say 'I hurt my ankle'?
questions.a: Say farsi male a: 'I made myself harm at the ankle'. It's reflexive, so use essere in the past.

examples.it: Mi sono fatto male alla caviglia.

questions.q: How do I say 'I need'?
questions.a: Use mi serve for one thing and mi servono for several: the thing needed is the subject, like piacere. Ho bisogno di also works.

questions.q: Can I drop 'that' or 'who' in 'the book I bought'?
questions.a: No. Italian always says che: il libro che ho comprato.

examples.it: Il libro che ho comprato è bello.
examples.en: The book I bought is good.

examples.it: La signora che lavora al bar è simpatica.
examples.en: The lady who works at the bar is nice.

questions.q: Che or cui?
questions.a: Che for the subject or direct object. Cui after a preposition: a cui, di cui, con cui, in cui.

examples.it: È l'amico di cui ti ho parlato.
examples.en: He's the friend I told you about.

examples.it: La ragazza con cui esco è di Napoli.
examples.en: The girl I go out with is from Naples.

questions.q: How do I say 'what' in 'I don't know what you want'?
questions.a: Use quello che or ciò che when 'what' means 'the thing that'.

examples.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

questions.q: How do I say 'those who' or 'whoever'?
questions.a: Use chi with a singular verb: chi studia means 'whoever studies' or 'those who study'.

questions.q: Più ... di or più ... che?
questions.a: Use di before a noun or pronoun (più alto di Marco). Use che when you compare two adjectives, verbs or phrases (più bello che comodo).

examples.it: Questo appartamento è più luminoso dell'altro.
examples.en: This flat is brighter than the other one.

questions.q: How do I say 'which' meaning 'and that'?
questions.a: When 'which' refers to a whole idea, use il che (or e questo).

examples.it: Parli molte lingue, il che è un vantaggio.
examples.en: You speak many languages, which is an advantage.

examples.it: Il treno era in ritardo, il che ci ha fatto perdere la coincidenza.
examples.en: The train was late, which made us miss our connection.

questions.q: When do I need 'had done' (the trapassato)?
questions.a: Whenever one past action happened before another past action, even if English would just say 'saw'. Italian is stricter about the order of tenses.

examples.it: Quando sono arrivato, il treno era già partito.
examples.en: When I arrived, the train had already left.

examples.it: Voleva sapere chi aveva visto lo studente.
examples.en: He wanted to know who had seen the student.

questions.q: What is the subjunctive, and when do I use it?
questions.a: It's a set of verb forms used after che when the main verb expresses an opinion, wish, fear, doubt or possibility. English gives you no signal, so look at the Italian main verb.

questions.q: Does 'I think that...' always take the subjunctive?
questions.a: After penso, credo, spero, voglio, temo and è possibile che, yes. After so che, dico che, sono sicuro che and è vero che, use the indicative.

questions.q: How do I say 'I want you to come'?
questions.a: Use volere che + subjunctive: 'I want that you come'. Only use the infinitive when the subject stays the same (voglio venire).

examples.it: Mia moglie vuole che io cucini.
examples.en: My wife wants me to cook.

questions.q: How do I say 'before' with a verb?
questions.a: Use prima di + infinitive when the subject is the same, and prima che + subjunctive when it's different. Before a noun, use prima di.

examples.en: Before I leave, I'll call you.

examples.it: Prima che tu parta, ti do le chiavi.
examples.en: Before you leave, I'll give you the keys.

questions.q: Which conjunctions take the subjunctive?
questions.a: Benché (although), perché meaning 'so that', prima che, purché and a condizione che (provided that). Anche se (even though) takes the indicative.

examples.it: Benché sia tardi, resto ancora un po'.
examples.en: Although it's late, I'll stay a bit longer.

examples.it: Te lo spiego perché tu capisca.
examples.en: I'll explain it so that you understand.

questions.q: Why 'qualche libro' and not 'qualche libri'?
questions.a: Qualche means 'some' but always takes a singular noun. For a plural, use alcuni / alcune or dei / delle.

questions.q: How do I say 'I miss you'?
questions.a: Use mancare, which works like piacere: 'you are lacking to me'. The person missed is the subject.

questions.q: How do I say 'If I were...'?
questions.a: Use se + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional. Never put the conditional after se.

examples.it: Se fossi ricco, comprerei una casa in Toscana.
examples.en: If I were rich, I'd buy a house in Tuscany.
If I had time, I'd come.

questions.q: What is the passato remoto?
questions.a: It's a one-word past used mostly in writing, history and storytelling (fu, nacque, costruirono). In conversation in the north and centre, the passato prossimo replaces it.

examples.it: La chiesa fu costruita nel Trecento.
examples.en: The church was built in the 1300s.

questions.q: How do I say 'was built by'?
questions.a: Use essere + the past participle, which agrees, and da for 'by'. In conversation Italians often use an active sentence or si instead.

examples.it: Il ponte è stato costruito dai Romani.
examples.en: The bridge was built by the Romans.

examples.it: Il conto è pagato dai genitori.
examples.en: The bill is paid by the parents.

questions.q: How do I say 'if only...!'?
questions.a: Use magari + imperfect subjunctive.

questions.q: How do I say 'If I had known, I would have come'?
questions.a: Use se + pluperfect subjunctive, then the past conditional.

examples.en: If I'd known, I would have come.

examples.it: Se avessimo avuto i soldi, saremmo partiti.
examples.en: If we'd had the money, we would have left.

questions.q: How do I say 'when I've finished, I'll...'?
questions.a: Use the future perfect (avrò / sarò + participle) for the action that comes first, after quando, dopo che or appena.

examples.en: When I've finished, I'll call you.

examples.it: Usciremo dopo che i bambini saranno andati a letto.
examples.en: We'll go out after the children have gone to bed.

questions.q: How do I say 'he said he would come'?
questions.a: Use the past conditional: ha detto che sarebbe venuto. English uses 'would come' here, but Italian needs 'would have come'.

examples.it: Paolo ha detto che sarebbe venuto.
Mi hai promesso che mi avresti aiutato.

questions.q: How do I say 'by studying' or 'while walking'?
questions.a: Use the gerundio (-ando, -endo) on its own, with no preposition before it.

examples.en: By studying hard, he learned Italian.

examples.it: Camminando, ho visto un vecchio amico.
examples.en: While walking, I saw an old friend.

questions.q: How do I say 'interesting' or 'surprising'?
questions.a: Adjectives like these often come from verbs and end in -ante or -ente. They work like ordinary -e adjectives.

questions.q: Why is Lei sometimes written with a capital L?
questions.a: Capital Lei, Le and Suo mark the polite 'you' in formal letters. In everyday writing, lowercase is common too.

examples.it: La ringrazio per la Sua risposta.

examples.en: I'm writing to ask for information.

questions.q: How do I say 'whose' in 'a poet whose works...'?
questions.a: Use the article + cui + noun. The article matches the thing owned.

examples.it: Dante è un poeta le cui opere sono famose.
examples.en: Dante is a poet whose works are famous.

examples.it: La casa il cui tetto è crollato.

recasts.why: How you are in health uses stare, not essere.
With someone you call signora, use the Lei form.
Lei takes the third-person verb, like 'she'.
Describing how you do something takes the adverb (-mente), not the adjective.
Italians say 'I call myself': mi chiamo.
Cities take a; countries and regions take in.
Countries take in, not a.
The adjective matches the person: feminine -a.
Uno is only for masculine words starting with z or s + consonant.
Before s + consonant, masculine words take uno.
Feminine una becomes un' before a vowel.
Masculine -o becomes -i in the plural.
Italian doesn't say 'it' as a subject; the verb is enough.
Italian links two nouns with a preposition: da for what something is for.
Age uses avere: 'I have thirty years'.
Pagare already includes 'for'.
Before s + consonant, masculine 'the' is lo.
Before s + consonant or a vowel, the masculine plural is gli.
After non, the 'some' word (del, della...) is dropped.
Cercare already means 'look for'.
There's no word for 'one': questo alone means 'this one'.
To point something out, use ecco; c'è says something exists.

recasts.en: Is there a pharmacy near here?
recasts.why: To ask whether something exists, use c'è.
Cos'è is the natural way to ask what something is.
'To someone's place' is da + the person.
Entrare needs in before the place.
Quanto matches the noun: quante for feminine plural.
Uovo has an irregular plural: le uova.
Problema is masculine even though it ends in -a.
For a choice among many (number, address), use qual è.
The thing liked is the subject: 'pizza is pleasing to me'.
The verb agrees with the thing liked: plural piacciono.
Weather uses fare.
Weather uses fare.
As a subject, English -ing is the Italian infinitive.
Bene (well) describes an action; buono (good) describes a thing.
A thing is buono; an action is done bene.

recasts.en: There are a lot of people.
recasts.why: Before a noun, molto agrees: molte persone.
English -ing adjectives become -ante or -ente.
Guardare already means 'look at'.
Italian never ends with a preposition: it goes before chi.
After a preposition, 'I' becomes me.
After a preposition, tu becomes te.
After volere, the infinitive follows directly.
For a learned skill, 'can' is sapere.
Aspettare already means 'wait for'.
Hunger uses avere: 'I have hunger'.
Thirst uses avere: 'I have thirst'.
Feeling cold uses avere.
The verb agrees with what hurts: plural fanno.
Andare takes essere in the past.
Essere takes essere in the past.
Mangiare takes avere in the past.
With essere, the participle matches the subject.
Visto is the everyday participle of vedere.
One family member takes no article, and possessives match the person's gender.
Possessives normally take the article.
The possessive matches the thing owned, not the owner.
Libri is masculine plural, so i suoi.
Loro never changes, but the article matches the thing: la.
'Hers' matches the brother, so masculine il suo.
Italian has no 's: say 'the car of John'.
'Whose' is di chi, 'of whom'.
Alone, 'that one' is quello; quel only goes before a noun.
The adjective matches the noun: feminine -a.
After essere, the adjective matches the subject.
After non, use the negative word: niente.
After non, use the negative word: nessuno.
'Never' needs non before the verb as well as mai.
For something ongoing over weeks or months, use the plain present.
Stare + -ando is only for right this minute.

recasts.wrong: Sto mangiando la pizza ogni sabato.
recasts.why: Habits take the plain present.
Alzarsi is reflexive: the mi can't be dropped.
Reflexive verbs take essere in the past.
'Have a good time' is divertirsi.
With piacere the person is 'to him': gli.
Piacere takes essere, and the film is the subject.
After a preposition, use the infinitive.

recasts.wrong: Da bambino sono andato al mare ogni estate.
recasts.right: Da bambino andavo al mare ogni estate.
recasts.en: As a child I used to go to the seaside every summer.
recasts.why: Habits in the past take the imperfetto.
Age in the past is description: imperfetto.
Time of day in the past takes the imperfetto.
Short object pronouns go before the conjugated verb.
With avere, the participle matches a lo/la placed before it.
Colour adjectives go after the noun.
Quello changes like the article: lo studente, quello studente.
Before a vowel the masculine plural is quegli, like gli.
Italian puts the main noun first: 'a racket for tennis'.
Telefonare takes a before the person.
Telefonare takes a, so 'him' is gli.
Telefonare takes a, so 'her' is le.
'To him' is gli; lo means 'him' as a direct object.
The participle doesn't agree with an indirect pronoun.
Telling a friend 'don't': non + infinitive.
The negative tu command is non + infinitive.

recasts.en: When you arrive, I'll call you.
recasts.why: Keep both halves in the future (or both in the present).

recasts.en: If I have the money, I'll come.
recasts.why: A real possibility takes present + present or future + future.
Before a name or noun, 'than' is di.
After a superlative, 'in' is di.

recasts.en: She would talk while he painted.
recasts.why: 'Would' meaning 'used to' is the imperfetto.
Italian never drops che.

recasts.en: The girl I go out with.
recasts.why: After a preposition use cui, and put the preposition first.

recasts.right: Il ragazzo di cui ho parlato.
recasts.why: Parlare di needs di + cui.

recasts.wrong: Voleva sapere chi ha visto lo studente.
recasts.right: Voleva sapere chi aveva visto lo studente.
recasts.en: He wanted to know who had seen the student.
recasts.why: The earlier past action takes the trapassato.
After penso che, use the subjunctive.
'Want someone to' is volere che + subjunctive.
After spero che, use the subjunctive.
With an infinitive, use prima di.
Prima che takes the subjunctive.
Qualche always takes a singular noun.

recasts.en: If I had time, I'd come.
recasts.why: After se, use the imperfect subjunctive, never the conditional.
Vorrei che takes the imperfect subjunctive.

recasts.wrong: Il ponte è stato costruito per i Romani.
recasts.right: Il ponte è stato costruito dai Romani.
recasts.en: The bridge was built by the Romans.
recasts.why: In the passive, 'by' is da, not per.

recasts.en: After they've eaten, we'll go out.
recasts.why: A future action completed first takes the future perfect.
With si, the verb agrees with what follows: plural.
A future seen from the past takes the past conditional.
The gerundio takes no preposition before it.
Fidarsi takes di.

steps: Familiar or formal? First names, friends, family, children → familiar. Signore, signora, a title, a stranger → formal. When in doubt, formal.
One person or more than one?
Choose: familiar one = tu; formal one = Lei (with the he/she verb form); more than one, familiar or formal = voi.

example.it: Signora, Lei viene con noi? Ragazzi, voi venite?
example.en: Madam, are you coming with us? Guys, are you coming?

steps: Find the conjugated verb.
Drop any English 'do / does / did' (and 'will' or 'would' if they only mark time).
Put non right before the verb (and before any short pronoun in front of it).

example.it: Non lo so. Non ho capito.
example.en: I don't know. I didn't understand.

steps: Start from the statement.
Drop 'do / does / did'; Italian has no question helper.
Raise your voice at the end, or put the subject after the verb (verb + rest + subject).
To check something, add vero? or no? at the end.

example.it: Studia italiano Giovanni? Sei di Roma, vero?
example.en: Is Giovanni studying Italian? You're from Rome, aren't you?

steps: Find the noun or person it describes.
Note its gender (masculine or feminine) and number (one or more).
Adjectives in -o have four endings: -o, -a, -i, -e. Adjectives in -e have two: -e (singular), -i (plural).
Put it after the noun, unless it's one of the short common ones that go before (bello, buono, grande, piccolo).

example.it: Le ragazze americane sono simpatiche.
example.en: The American girls are nice.

steps: Look at the ending: -o is usually masculine, -a usually feminine.
Consonant ending (bar, film, sport) → masculine.
-zione, -tà, -tù, -ie → feminine; -i is usually feminine (la crisi).
-e → could be either: learn it with its article.
Watch the exceptions: il problema, la mano, la foto, la radio.

example.it: il latte, la lezione
example.en: the milk, the lesson

steps: Is the noun masculine or feminine?
Look at its first letter.
Masculine: uno before z or s + consonant; un before everything else, vowels included.
Feminine: un' before a vowel; una before a consonant.

example.it: un caffè, uno spritz, una birra, un'aranciata
example.en: a coffee, a spritz, a beer, an orange soda

steps: Look at the last letter.
-o → -i; -e → -i; -a (feminine) → -e.
Ends in an accented vowel, a consonant or -i → no change; let the article show the plural.
Change the article and any adjective to match.

example.it: il cornetto caldo → i cornetti caldi; il caffè → i caffè
example.en: the warm croissant → the warm croissants; the coffee → the coffees

steps: Gender: masculine or feminine?
Number: one or more?
First sound of the next word: vowel; z or s + consonant; other consonant.
Masculine: il / i before most consonants; lo / gli before z or s + consonant; l' / gli before a vowel.
Feminine: la / le before a consonant; l' / le before a vowel.

example.it: il pane, lo zucchero, l'olio, gli spaghetti, la pasta, le uova
example.en: the bread, the sugar, the oil, the spaghetti, the pasta, the eggs

steps: Is the sentence negative? Then leave 'some' out: non ho pane.
Is it a question? 'Some' is optional.
Otherwise use di + the right 'the': del, dello, dell', della (one mass noun), dei, degli, delle (several countable things).
Un po' di is always a safe alternative.

example.it: Vorrei del pane e delle pesche.
example.en: I'd like some bread and some peaches.

steps: Find the noun you mean.
Note its gender and number.
Choose questo, questa, questi, queste (near) or quello, quella, quelli, quelle (far). Add no word for 'one'.

example.it: Quale borsa? Questa, non quella.
example.en: Which bag? This one, not that one.

recipes.for: choosing a preposition for a place
steps: A city or town → a (abito a Napoli, vado a Napoli).
A country, region or large island → in (in Italia, in Sicilia).
A person or their home or business → da (dal medico, da Luca).
A room or a shop named by its type → in (in cucina, in farmacia).
The same preposition means 'in', 'at' and 'to'.

example.it: Domani vado a Bologna, poi in Toscana da mia sorella.
example.en: Tomorrow I'm going to Bologna, then to Tuscany to my sister's.

recipes.for: choosing che, quale or quanto before a noun
steps: General 'what + noun' → che (never changes).
'Which one(s) of these' → quale (singular) or quali (plural).
'How much / how many' → quanto, quanta, quanti, quante, matching the noun's gender and number.

example.it: Quante pesche vuole? E quale melone?
example.en: How many peaches would you like? And which melon?

recipes.for: saying 'how much / how many' without a noun
steps: Find the noun it stands for.
Note its gender.
Note its number.
Choose quanto, quanta, quanti or quante.

example.it: C'erano dieci studenti. Quanti hanno votato?
example.en: There were ten students. How many voted?

steps: Do you want a definition or explanation? → Cos'è...?
Do you want one answer out of many possible ones (a name, number, address, favourite)? → Qual è...? (Quali sono...? for several.)

example.it: Cos'è la ribollita? Qual è il tuo piatto preferito?
example.en: What's ribollita? What's your favourite dish?

recipes.for: conjugating a regular verb in the present
steps: Find the group from the infinitive: -are, -ere or -ire.
Find the stem: take off the -are, -ere or -ire.
Find the subject (ask 'who is doing it?'); X and I = noi, you and X = voi, two others = loro.
Add the ending: -are: -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano; -ere: -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono; -ire: -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ite, -ono.
Leave out the subject pronoun unless you need emphasis or clarity.

example.it: Io e Marco parliamo; tu e Anna parlate.
example.en: Marco and I talk; you and Anna talk.

steps: Turn the English round: 'I like the car' → 'the car is pleasing to me'.
The person becomes 'to me / to you / to him': mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, gli (or a + name).
Put that person first.
The thing liked is the subject: piace for one thing or a verb, piacciono for several.

example.it: A Carlo piace la macchina. Mi piacciono i musei.
example.en: Carlo likes the car. I like museums.

steps: Ask what the word describes.
A noun → adjective: it agrees (buono, buona; molti, molte).
A verb, an adjective or another adverb → adverb: it never changes (bene, molto, lentamente).

example.it: È una buona macchina e va bene. È molto bella.
example.en: It's a good car and it runs well. It's very nice.

recipes.for: asking a question with a preposition
steps: Find the English preposition, often stranded at the end ('Who are you going with?').
Restructure so it comes first: 'With whom are you going?'.
Translate: preposition + chi (people), cosa (things) or quale/quali (which).

example.it: Con chi vai? Di cosa parlate?
example.en: Who are you going with? What are you talking about?

recipes.for: choosing a pronoun after a preposition
steps: Find the preposition (con, per, di, da, a, senza...).
Choose the strong form: me, te, lui, lei, Lei, noi, voi, loro.
For 'you': familiar one = te; formal one = Lei; more than one = voi.

example.it: Vengo con te. Questo è per Lei, signora.
example.en: I'm coming with you. This is for you, madam.

recipes.for: finding the right verb for an English verb + preposition
steps: Look up the whole English phrase (look for, look after, wait for), not just the verb.
Take the Italian verb it gives (cercare, badare a, aspettare); don't add the English preposition.
Check whether the Italian verb itself needs a preposition (telefonare a, entrare in, fidarsi di).
That tells you what kind of object or pronoun follows.

example.it: Cerco Franco. Entro in classe. Telefono a Maria.
example.en: I'm looking for Franco. I go into the classroom. I'm calling Maria.

recipes.for: saying 'X is done / one does X' with si
steps: Find the thing being done to (tickets, English).
Put si before the verb in the third person.
Make the verb agree with that thing: singular (si vende) or plural (si vendono).

example.it: Qui si parla inglese. Dove si comprano i biglietti?
example.en: English is spoken here. Where do you buy tickets?

steps: Exists or is there? → c'è / ci sono.
Pointing at it ('there it is!')? → ecco.
Hunger, thirst, sleepiness, cold, heat, fear, age? → avere (ho fame, ho trent'anni).
Weather? → fare (fa caldo).
Health ('how are you')? → stare (sto bene).
Otherwise → essere.

example.it: Ho freddo: fa freddo oggi, ma sto bene.
example.en: I'm cold: it's cold today, but I'm fine.

recipes.for: choosing avere or essere in the past
steps: Does the verb take a direct object (eat something, see someone)? → avere.
Is it reflexive (alzarsi, divertirsi)? → essere.

Otherwise check the essere list: andare / venire, arrivare / partire, entrare / uscire, nascere / morire, essere, stare, restare, diventare, piacere, riuscire. If it's on the list → essere; if not → avere.
Unsure? The dictionary shows the auxiliary.

example.it: Ho mangiato e poi sono uscito.
example.en: I ate and then I went out.

steps: Turn the English round: 'John's shirt' → 'the shirt of John'.
Put the thing owned first, with its article.
Add di + the owner; if the owner has an article, merge them (del, della, dei, delle).
With no noun ('my father's'), use quello / quella / quelli / quelle di, matched to the thing.

example.it: la camicia di Giovanni; Quale casa? Quella di mio padre.
example.en: John's shirt; Which house? My father's.

steps: Find the thing owned and note its gender and number.
Find the owner, which gives the stem: mi- (my), tu- (your, one friend), su- (his, her, its, formal your), nostr- (our), vostr- (your, several), loro (their).
Add the article that matches the thing owned.
Add the ending that matches the thing: -o, -a, -i, -e (mio → miei, tuo → tuoi, suo → suoi; loro never changes).
Check everything agrees. With one family member, drop the article (mia madre).

example.it: i miei libri, la sua casa, le loro figlie
example.en: my books, his/her house, their daughters

steps: Find the thing it stands for and note its gender and number.
Choose the possessive as for 'my' (mio, tuo, suo...), matched to that thing, not the owner.
Add the article (il mio, la tua...). After essere, it's usually dropped (è mio).

example.it: Questa è la mia chiave; loro hanno dimenticato la loro.
example.en: Here's my key; they forgot theirs.

steps: Restructure: 'whose car is it?' → 'of whom is the car?'.
Di chi + è (one thing) or sono (several) + the thing.

example.it: Di chi sono queste chiavi?
example.en: Whose keys are these?

recipes.for: using a negative word (nothing, nobody, never)
steps: Find the English indefinite word (anything, anyone, ever, anywhere).
Choose its negative opposite: niente, nessuno, mai, da nessuna parte.
Restructure the English as a double negative: 'I don't see nobody'.
Say non + verb + the negative word.

example.it: Non vedo nessuno. Non ho mangiato niente.
example.en: I don't see anyone. I haven't eaten anything.

steps: Is it happening right this minute, and do you want to stress that? → sto, stai, sta + -ando (-are) or -endo (-ere, -ire).
Is it a habit, a general truth, or something going on these days or this year? → plain present.

example.it: Cosa studi quest'anno? Adesso sto studiando.
example.en: What are you studying this year? Right now I'm studying.

steps: Spot the -si infinitive (alzarsi, chiamarsi, divertirsi).
Choose the pronoun for the subject: mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si.
Put it before the conjugated verb.
In the past, use essere and make the participle agree with the subject.

example.it: Mi alzo alle sette. Ieri mi sono alzata alle nove.
example.en: I get up at seven. Yesterday I got up at nine.

steps: Does English say or mean 'used to'? → imperfetto.
Does English say 'was / were -ing'? → imperfetto.
Is it a description: age, weather, time, feelings, how things were? → imperfetto.
Is it a finished event: what happened, once or a set number of times? → passato prossimo.
In one sentence, the background is imperfetto and the event that interrupts it is passato prossimo.

example.it: Pioveva quando sono uscito.
example.en: It was raining when I went out.

steps: Is it a noun (subject, or after a preposition or piacere)? → infinitive: leggere è bello; prima di partire; mi piace nuotare.
Is it part of 'is / was -ing'? → plain present or imperfetto; stare + -ando only for 'right now'.
Is it a 'by / while doing' phrase? → gerundio (-ando, -endo), no preposition.
Is it an adjective (interesting)? → -ante or -ente adjective.

example.it: Prima di partire, mi piace camminare.
example.en: Before leaving, I like walking.

steps: Find the noun it stands for (the antecedent).
Note its gender.
Note its number.
Choose lo (m. sing.), la (f. sing.), li (m. pl.), le (f. pl.).
Put it before the conjugated verb (or attach it to an infinitive).

example.it: Vedi la macchina? Sì, la vedo.
example.en: Do you see the car? Yes, I see it.

steps: Which auxiliary? Essere → the participle agrees with the subject.
Avere → is there a lo, la, li or le before the verb? Then it agrees with that pronoun.
Otherwise (avere with no direct pronoun in front, or an indirect pronoun like le or gli) → leave it in -o.

example.it: Maria è partita. Le chiavi? Le ho prese. Le ho parlato.
example.en: Maria has left. The keys? I took them. I spoke to her.

steps: Note the noun's gender and number.
Look at its first letter, exactly as for 'the'.
Masculine: quel / quei (most consonants), quello / quegli (z, s + consonant), quell' / quegli (vowel).
Feminine: quella / quelle; quell' before a vowel.

example.it: quel ragazzo, quello studente, quell'albero, quegli alberi
example.en: that boy, that student, that tree, those trees

steps: Familiar or formal?
One person or more?
Direct ('see you'): ti (one, familiar), La (one, formal), vi (several).
Indirect ('to you'): ti (one, familiar), Le (one, formal), vi (several).
After a preposition: te, Lei, voi.

example.it: Signora, La chiamo domani e Le spiego tutto.
example.en: Madam, I'll call you tomorrow and explain everything to you.

recipes.for: choosing an indirect object pronoun ('to him, to her')
steps: Check that the Italian verb takes a (dare a, telefonare a, scrivere a, piacere a), whatever English does.
Find the person.
Choose: mi, ti, gli (to him), le (to her), Le (to you, formal), ci, vi, gli (to them).
Drop the 'to' and put the pronoun before the conjugated verb.

example.it: Gli do il libro. Le telefono stasera.
example.en: I'll give him the book. I'll call her tonight.

recipes.for: working out what kind of object an Italian verb takes
steps: Look up the Italian verb, not the English one.
No preposition (cercare, aspettare, guardare, pagare) → direct object: lo, la, li, le.
With a (telefonare a, somigliare a) → indirect object: gli, le.
With another preposition (ricordarsi di, fidarsi di, entrare in) → keep that preposition + noun or strong pronoun.
Turned round, like piacere, mancare, dispiacere, servire → the English subject becomes 'to me / to him'.

example.it: Aspetto Marco. Gli telefono. Mi fido di lui. Mi manca.
example.en: I'm waiting for Marco. I'll call him. I trust him. I miss him.

steps: Is there emphasis or a contrast ('her, not him')?
No → short pronoun before the verb (la vedo, le do il libro).
Yes → strong pronoun after the verb (vedo lei, do il libro a lei).

example.it: Non cerco lui, cerco lei.
example.en: I'm not looking for him, I'm looking for her.

steps: Who are you telling? One friend, several people, 'let's', or someone you call Lei?
Tu: -are verbs end in -a (parla), -ere and -ire verbs end in -i (scrivi, parti).
Tu negative: non + infinitive (non parlare).
Voi and noi: same as the present (parlate, andiamo); negative just adds non.
Lei: the subjunctive form (parli, scriva, parta); negative just adds non.

example.it: Gira a destra! Non correre! Andiamo! Scusi, signora.
example.en: Turn right! Don't run! Let's go! Excuse me, madam.

steps: Start from the infinitive.
-are verbs: change -are to -er- (parlare → parler-).
-ere and -ire verbs: drop the final -e (prendere → prender-, partire → partir-).
Learn the short stems: andr-, avr-, sar-, far-, verr-, potr-, vorr-.
Add -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno.

example.it: Domani parlerò con lui e poi partirò.
example.en: Tomorrow I'll talk to him and then I'll leave.

recipes.for: the tense after 'when' / 'as soon as' about the future
steps: Is the action after quando / appena / se in the future?
Then put it in the future too, where English uses the present.
If it will be finished before the main action, use the future perfect (avrò fatto).
In casual speech, both halves in the present is also fine.

example.it: Appena arriverò, ti chiamerò.
example.en: As soon as I arrive, I'll call you.

steps: More than → più + adjective + di (di + article merges: del, della).
Less than → meno + adjective + di.
As ... as → (così) + adjective + come, or (tanto) + adjective + quanto.
The most / the least → il / la / i / le più (meno) + adjective + di; 'in' after a superlative is di.
Very → -issimo or molto + adjective. Learn migliore / peggiore separately.

example.it: Roma è più grande di Firenze, ma Firenze è bellissima.
example.en: Rome is bigger than Florence, but Florence is beautiful.

steps: Take the future stem (parler-, prender-, partir-; vorr-, potr-, dovr-, sar-, avr-).
Add -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero.

example.it: Vorrei un tavolo per due. Potrebbe aiutarmi?
example.en: I'd like a table for two. Could you help me?

steps: Does 'would' mean 'used to' (a past habit)? → imperfetto.
Is it a future seen from the past ('said he would come')? → past conditional (sarebbe venuto).
Is it in the 'if' half of a sentence? → never the conditional; use the subjunctive.
Otherwise (polite requests, wishes, 'would' results) → conditional.

example.it: Da piccolo mangiavo sempre il gelato; ora vorrei un caffè.
example.en: As a child I would always eat ice cream; now I'd like a coffee.

recipes.for: choosing a relative pronoun (that, who, which, whom)
steps: Find the relative clause; if a preposition dangles at the end, move it to the front ('the student I talked about' → 'about whom I talked').
Find or put back the relative pronoun; Italian never leaves it out.
Find the antecedent (the noun it refers to). Person or thing doesn't matter.

Decide its job in the Italian clause: subject or direct object → che; after a (to whom) → a cui; after another preposition → preposition + cui; 'whose' → article + cui + noun (article matches the thing owned).
Choose the form.

example.it: I ragazzi di cui parlavamo erano giovani.
example.en: The boys we were talking about were young.

recipes.for: relatives with no antecedent (what, which, those who)
steps: Does 'what' mean 'the thing that'? → quello che / ciò che.
Does 'which' refer to a whole idea in the sentence before? → il che.
Does it mean 'he who / those who / whoever'? → chi + singular verb.

example.it: Non so quello che vuoi. Chi cerca trova.
example.en: I don't know what you want. Whoever looks will find.

steps: Put the past events on a timeline: now = 0, the main past event = -1.
Is there an action that happened before -1? That's -2.
Put -2 in the trapassato: imperfetto of avere or essere + past participle, with the same auxiliary choice and agreement as the passato prossimo.
Do this even if English just uses the simple past.

example.it: Quando sono arrivata, il film era già cominciato.
example.en: When I arrived, the film had already started.

steps: Find the main verb or expression before che.
Opinion, wish, hope, fear, doubt, emotion, command or possibility (penso, credo, spero, voglio, temo, è possibile, è importante)? → subjunctive.
Knowledge or certainty (so, dico, sono sicuro, è vero, secondo me)? → indicative.
Same subject in both parts? → di + infinitive instead (spero di venire).

example.it: Credo che sia tardi, ma so che hai tempo.
example.en: I think it's late, but I know you have time.

steps: Is 'before' followed by a noun? → prima di (+ article): prima della cena.
Followed by a verb with the same subject? → prima di + infinitive.
Followed by a clause with a different subject? → prima che + subjunctive.

example.it: Prima di cena ti chiamo, prima che tu esca.
example.en: I'll call you before dinner, before you go out.

steps: Is it a real possibility? → se + present, then present (or future + future).
Is it unreal now ('if I were')? → se + imperfect subjunctive, then present conditional.
Is it unreal in the past ('if I had')? → se + pluperfect subjunctive, then past conditional (B2).
Never put the conditional right after se.

example.it: Se ho tempo vengo; se avessi tempo verrei.
example.en: If I have time I'll come; if I had time I'd come.

recipes.for: turning an active sentence into a passive one
steps: The direct object becomes the subject.
Put essere in the same tense as the active verb, + the past participle, matching the new subject.
The old subject, if you keep it, follows da (dal, dalla...).
Ask whether si + verb or an active sentence would sound more natural; Italian uses the passive less than English.

example.it: Il professore prepara l'esame → L'esame è preparato dal professore.
example.en: The teacher prepares the exam → The exam is prepared by the teacher.

recipes.for: reporting what someone said in the past
steps: Is the reporting verb in the past (ha detto, diceva)?
Present → imperfetto; passato prossimo → trapassato.
Future (or 'would' about later) → past conditional: sarebbe venuto.
If the reporting verb is present (dice), change nothing.

example.it: Ha detto che sarebbe venuto alle otto.
example.en: He said he would come at eight.
